EFFECT OF EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY DECREE ON HORSE MEAT PLANTS IN CANADA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the European Economic Community has issued a decree that, as of June 30 of this year, it will require a certificate stating that all fresh and frozen horse meat exported from Canada must come from horses which were located in Canada for at least three months before slaughter, a decree which will put all horse abattoirs in Canada out of business since at least 80 per cent of slaughter horses come from the United States, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Kushner):
That the government make the strongest protest possible to the European Economic Community to withdraw this decree which would have such a devastating effect on the viability of all our horse meat plants throughout Canada.

speechtext:

We have established a very open and very compassionate immigration law which sets out proper procedures by which people can come to Canada. Our record is second to none in the world in providing a very open invitation and welcome. However, many people come here illegally and we provide some response to them in a compassionate way. subsubtopic: QUEBEC IMPORTS AND EXPORTS
speechtext: What was the value of Quebec imports and exports with (a) the Atlantic provinces (b) Ontario (c) the prairie provinces (d) British Columbia (e) the territories (f) foreign countries, for the year 1979 or the latest year for which such information is available?

subsubtopic: QUEBEC IMPORTS AND EXPORTS
speechtext: Statistics Canada reports that there is no comprehensive set of data available at this time on the value of Quebec imports and exports by region of Canada and the rest of the world. Administrative systems have not been designed to capture interprovincial trade data, nor are provinces identified in international trade statistics. The provincial economic accounts published by Statistics Canada estimates the aggregate provincial net export as a residual and sheds no light on interprovincial import/export. A project initiated in May, 1979, to estimate commodity detail of provincial trade holds promise of supplying interprovincial trade data, but results are not yet available. Some information of oblique pertinence to the question is implicit in the 1967, 1974 and 1979 surveys of origin and destination of manufacturers shipments in transportation surveys. But the analysis needed to focus this information onto the particular question is not available and would be complex.

subsubtopic: DND-CONTRACT WITH UNIVERSITY OF B.C.
speechtext: Did the Department of National Defence place a contract for $23,541 with the University of British Columbia to develop a life quality improvement program data bank and, if so, what exactly is the life quality improvement program and what is the purpose of the data bank?

subsubtopic: DND-CONTRACT WITH UNIVERSITY OF B.C.
speechtext: On December 29, 1980, the Department of Supply and Services awarded a contract to the University of British Columbia on behalf of the Department of National Defence for the investigation into the development of a Life Quality Improvement Program (LQIP) Data Bank for $23,541.00. The Life Quality Improvement Program is a preventive medicine program designed to shift emphasis from costly diagnosis and cure of disease to the hopefully more cost-effective identification and reduction of health risks for a given population. The purpose of the data bank is to integrate accumulated results from divergent sources including departmental fitness programs, smoking cessation research and lifestyle patterning research at various Canadian universities and government agencies.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 20, consideration of Bill C-59, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and on the motion of Mr. Blenkarn (p. 8463).

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) take his seat. I was afraid I would be speaking in the absence of someone representing that department today. When we were last in this House, we were talking about a juggling act, and I am very impressed with the act being performed by this government.
The day this debate was cut off, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) referred to our desire to eliminate increased expenditure on social programs. The reason increases are required is that this government's spending programs are out of control, and inflation causes increased spending.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Ridiculous.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
We are not against social programs, but we are against increased government spending. This government is perpetrating a continuous fraud on the Canadian public. This fraud would not be permitted in any other part of the world. If the government was a corporation, the board of directors would be thrown out. In other democracies the government would be thrown out. That is what should be done.
This government has the nerve to come before this House and ask for $14 billion. It already has $4.8 billion in the bank. That would give it a total of $18.8 billion. It is bad enough that it anticipates a deficit of $14 billion, but now it says that it will have to borrow $18.8 billion to keep this country afloat.
I am not surprised the government was wrong about inflation. It is like shooting a gun into the sky. This government is an absolute glutton pretending to be on a diet.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
It has absolutely no respect for the taxpayers of this country. It is the money of the taxpayers which the

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 government is spending, not the government's. It has not earned it.
In view of this hoard of money which is sitting in the Bank of Canada, it is my opinion that the government should reconsider its request to this Parliament and that our party should reconsider our amendment. We should not even allow it to have $8 billion; we should cut the amount down to $3.2 billion. We should make the government consider how it will spend the money before it squanders it on our behalf.
Every time the government borrows excess funds-which it is doing right now-it destroys the opportunity for industry to raise funds at reasonable rates. It destroys the housing industry. People cannot afford to pay the interest on mortgages. It eliminates the possibility for Canadians to become home owners, which is their one great dream.
Government borrowing creates inflation which is erasing the value of the savings of senior citizens. This is referred to in the pensions conference which is taking place. The government will index that next. The only reason for indexing is that this government knows how to throw its money away.
In our opinion, this government is totally inept and incompetent. This is very clearly exemplified in this bill. Its ineptness is also clearly shown in the energy program which has been presented and which it will now hopefully have to backtrack on.
The government cannot throw the blame for having to borrow this money on to us because we were only in government for nine months. It is necessitated by a series of incompetent budgets presented by the Liberal government since 1968. In those budgets and in its requests for funds, it has never requested funds to help industry. It only borrows funds to spend. What are we doing for industrial development in this country? What has the government done in 13 years? Nothing. Does the government realize that at current rates of interest, without any additional borrowing, if it stopped today and said that it would not borrow any more money, our debt would amount to $200 billion by 1986? That would be the result if we voted in this House not to permit any further borrowing; our debt would still be $200 billion. That is assuming there were no additional deficits and that the government did not require any money. That is assuming the interest rate, which is now in place because of this inflationary spiral, continues.
Furthermore, does the government realize that by 1986-is less than five years away-the interest to carry this debt will amount to $1,000 for each man, woman and child in this country? Let us assume that an average Canadian family consists of 3.5 people, a mother and father and 1.5 children. Assuming that, the amount of $3,500 has to be brought home by the wage earner just for the government to pay the bill. That is assuming we have a balanced budget and that we are not carrying on with this throw-away program with which the government has been doing so well. I plead with the government to stop coming back to the trough. We are destroying ourselves and our country. We must stop doing that and we
must stop now. We have run out of goodwill overseas. Where do we go next to borrow money if we are turned down?
The government keeps borrowing additional sums to buy up private corporations. Do hon. members realize that every time a private corporation is purchased a taxpayer is eliminated? Once a company becomes a Crown corporation, it does not earn any money. That is why we are borrowing more money- to buy corporations that can become non-profit organizations. Such a procedure erodes our tax base. It erodes the chance for this country to have a balanced budget.
I maintain it is time for the government to stop borrowing money and start to encourage the private sector instead. Productivity should be increased, and this will result in increased revenue, eliminating the need to borrow money. If a corporation were to carry on in this way, it would go broke. A good example is Chrysler. The government had to bail out Chrysler. That was just another example of throwing money away. In the case of Massey-Ferguson, which kept borrowing too much money, again the government had to bail the company out. But let me ask hon. members this: Who is going to bail out the government?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: The citizens.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: If the government would be reasonable with its energy program and let the price of oil go to 75 per cent of world prices, levy a logical tax on oil instead of the Mickey Mouse taxes the government keeps pushing around, we would have revenues accruing to the government. This would eliminate the necessity to borrow more money. The government has this grandiose economic idea that it does not matter how much money we borrow because we can carry on. The government has no desire to restrict expenditures. It does nothing to earn money. The government has never tried to earn money, nor has it ever tried to save money. The government just likes to spend money.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: Other people's money.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext: A good example, again concerning energy, is that the government has encouraged Canadians to continue to buy gas guzzlers. As a result, Canadian manufacturers have not made small vehicles. No one wanted them. Then all of a sudden, who got caught with their pants down? The government did. I will acknowledge that. However, if the government had faced reality in 1973, the auto industry today would be healthy. Chrysler would not be in the position of having to be bailed out. If the government had allowed the logical sequence to occur, then all the gas guzzlers would have hit the scrapyards and we would be driving cars we hope we will see by 1986. The only reason small cars will be manufactured in this country is that our friends to the south of us had enough sense to realize it is the only way to eliminate excessive use of gasoline.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
What kind of a car do you drive?
April 3, 1981

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I drive a very economical car. It is called an Omni. There is a plant in my constituency that produces Omnis. Because the Americans will accept world prices for gasoline by 1983-1984, this will have an impact on the cars we buy. It will help production of our cars. But what have we done for ourselves? We have done absolutely nothing.
The government keeps boasting about the employment it has created in Canada. The government has not created any additional employment. It employs many people, and every time the government employs additional people, Mr. Speaker, it simply increases our deficit. This is not productive. It does not produce cars, nor does it produce wheat. It does not produce anything except a bunch of bureaucratic servants in Ottawa.
I suggest that this government should be innovative. It should start an exchange program for civil servants. It should send those people out to the private sector, so long as the private sector can stand them. The government should send these people out to the private sector for two years. They may then learn by experience and by being exposed to the private sector how hard it is to make a buck. These people may then reconsider their free-wheeling, give-away programs. I come from the private sector and I can say I have been successful, but I had to work hard. I would love to employ a civil servant and let him know what it really means to make money and how hard it is to make it. He will then understand that he should not be quite so free in giving money away. What the government is doing is immoral. The government is taking money right out of the Canadian people's pockets. It is not taking it from welfare recipients or from people who do not want to work; it is taking it out of the guts of Canadians, those people who pay the bills.
Many times in this House I have compared the Canadian small business program with the American small business program. What have we done to face the industrial problem in this country? Why do we not plagiarize something that is beneficial? The small business program in the United States has worked well. Small industries are growing throughout small towns in the United States. Why does the government not look at what the United States has done? If the government brought forward a borrowing bill in that regard, I would support it wholeheartedly. I would be behind the government and would do everything to encourage it. I would find people who would be interested in entering the manufacturing sector of Canada. We should stop exporting our raw materials. I would be one hundred per cent behind the government if it did that, and I think hon. members can appreciate that. This is a way to get the country moving. I tell the government to stop purchasing the private sector now. Let the private sector carry on by itself. The private sector can look after itself.
Free enterprise is the right to win and the right to lose. I do not believe we should subsidize free enterprise. Although I believe we should help free enterprise, I do not necessarily agree with what this country has done in the past. Free enterprisers should either swing and be successful or they should fail. But the government must not carry on subsidizing
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
or purchasing private industry. Whenever the government purchases private enterprise, all it is doing is putting money in other people's pockets. In a most recent case, many Belgians will become very rich from our great endeavour in broadening the base of Petro-Canada.
The government should take a good look at what has happened. The government should be directing the way in foreign affairs and equalization. It should be looking after those people who are incapable of looking after themselves. But I say to the government, do not keep treading on everybody and eroding the base on which this country is built.
I am proud when Air Canada makes a profit, but Canadian Pacific has to make a profit or it will go out of business. If a Crown corporation cannot make a profit, I maintain it should be disbanded. I am talking about Crown corporations directly in competition with the private sector, not Crown corporations established from an essential or a security point of view. I say allow the private sector to operate in the real world. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stated, I believe in the last election campaign: "The gradual reduction of inflation and interest rates is the only viable solution to the problem." The government's spending is out of control and he has not put a lid on it at this time. Do the government really know the consequences of the borrowing authority they are asking for? Do they really care, or is their only purpose to get through the next election?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in this debate, not because I am happy we are dealing with the bill but because I am happy to express some concerns I have about the way the government spends taxpayers' dollars.
To begin, I think it is fair to say that even including the constitutional debate, more people have raised with me the expenditure of tax dollars by the government and the heavy borrowing the government has now undertaken as a matter of course than any other single topic we have had before us in the last year and two months.
I know from canvassing my constituency, travelling around this province and across the country that a great deal of concern is being expressed, and rightly so, by the people of Canada about the future of this country, its economy and the way in which it is being managed or not managed, and the problems of an ever-increasing tax burden on average wage earners. The majority of people have put the case very well. You cannot expect the average wage earner to assume an ever-larger share of the indebtedness caused by government expenditure if his wages consistently fall behind the increasing cost of living.
That has been the case over the course of the last few years. People are earning less in comparison to the impact of inflation and the increasing cost of living. The government is contributing to the decline in disposable income of the average family in Canada as a result of the policy pursued through this bill and the policies it pursues in terms of its over-all economic strategy.
It is important that we give serious thought to the over-all effect of continuing this kind of carte blanche borrowing authority, given without any consideration being placed before the House of Commons as to the purpose and without any careful analysis having been made of the impact on the money markets and the economic growth of this country. I want to say categorically that economic growth cannot be maintained or enhanced by an ever-increasing debt load.
The government cannot and must not encourage unnecessary borrowing in the money markets. As government borrows ever-increasing larger sums of money from what is considered by most analysts a finite market, the end result is that the cost of money is driven up. It influences the availability of funds for small and not so small enterprises. It detrimentally affects the
capacity of wage earners to borrow for necessary purchases because the cost of borrowing goes beyond the ability of the average family to repay. No matter what your philosophy or ideology, there are some things that are true and irrefutable and therefore have to be given a great deal of consideration by the House of Commons.
In looking at this bill and the amendment before us we have to recognize, as I said last night, that this bill should not be dealt with in haste. It is far too important to be dealt with in isolation from all other economic considerations and in haste.
I personally believe that the government ought not to be given the amount of money it is asking for. That does not mean I do not understand the necessity to be able to borrow. However, I do not think the government needs, nor should it ask for, a full year's borrowing allowance from the House of Commons. The government should be prepared to come back to the House of Commons, at the bare minimum, every six months to justify both the expenditure levels and the amount of borrowing that must take place. The government must be prepared to come back and allow a more careful analysis of the economic conditions which exist at the time the borrowing is required in order that we can understand the way in which that money is to be used and the way in which we will budget over the course of time for its repayment.
I hate to argue this again as I argued it in another House at another time, but the government should not ask for 12 months' borrowing authority. Neither should it request that it be allowed to carry over unused borrowing powers. We should insist, as Members of Parliament charged with the responsibility of challenging the expenditures of government, that before any approval is given at any time the government should justify its request, not only in terms of use but also in terms of the way in which it will ultimately repay it.
I can see no fundamental justification for moving from $14 billion to $8 billion, so for that reason I am prepared to support the amendment. We should allow the government less latitude rather than more in the amount of indebtedness it incurs on behalf of the people of the country.
I also think it is a flagrant disregard of the obligations of parliamentarians to expect that we will at the early part of a fiscal year give the government the unfettered right to go out and borrow for whatever purpose it sees fit. I cannot support that as a principle which withstands the test of the process for which Parliament was intended to serve.
I have looked at the problems of borrowing. I have believed for years that we have unnecessarily encouraged indebtedness. Let us consider credit cards. My God, who does not have them? We have credit cards without any checks and balances which have permitted people to extend their borrowing far in excess of their ability to pay.

speechtext:
Even in Scotland? That was a very intelligent interjection. I thought the hon. member was saying something important.
The interesting thing about this is that because it is possible for an individual in the country to carry far more than one credit card with limits on each, and to borrow without any cross-reference, we have allowed and encouraged individual citizens to incur debts they frankly cannot afford. The end result of that we can see in every bankruptcy court across the country. We can see people being put into the position of declaring bankruptcy when up until a few years ago they would never have considered the possibility of being forced to do that.
For a long time I have felt that a person in this country requires but one credit card, if one is required at all. The spending limit, calculated on the basis of their indebtedness and obligations, should appear on the face of the credit card. With one phone call it would be possible to check whether a person had exceeded or was almost at the limit of his credit in order that he does not fall into the trap of borrowing beyond his means.
You cannot impose that on the public, even if it is decided that that is in their best interests, unless you are prepared to exercise the same kind of control, caution and care when the government borrows and commits the public of Canada to an ever-increasing tax burden to meet whatever the government decides are the expenditure priorities which fit its particular political mood at the time.
The end result of this kind of bill, which comes before the House of Commons and every legislative assembly almost every year-certainly I cannot think of a situation in which it does not occur-with the pressure this exerts on the money market and money markets of the world, is that others must pay ever higher interest rates. Those higher interest rates are reflected in higher prices and in higher domestic interest rates. Those higher prices and higher domestic interest rates reduce the amount of expendable capital. That reduction in the amount of expendable capital means a reduction in the manufacturing sector because of the reduction in the amount of purchasing which takes place. The end result of that, of course, is that fewer people are required to work. Manufacturers for a while carry a larger inventory, but the cost of carrying that inventory pushes prices up even further. The end result of all that is that there is less available capital in the country. What we see then is the government, because it cannot raise the money it believes it requires through the tax structure, going back to the market place to borrow even more, and the process starts all over again.
Therefore, what I am suggesting to the government, through you, Mr. Speaker, is that we desperately need an opportunity to take a look at the over-all fiscal and monetary policies of the government, and not only of this government. I might say that this is probably true of almost every jurisdiction in this country. I think it is necessary when dumping on the government, as it is the opposition's bent to do, to recognize that the government is allowed to get into these sloppy habits by a
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
House of Commons which does not demand that it respond properly and adequately to the needs, desires, wishes and requirements, if you will, of the electorate, the people who must ultimately pay the bills.
We will not support the bill. We will support the amendment and I suggest the amendment should carry. I hope the government will pay heed to my plea that we not be required to give a full year's approval, but rather that we restrict it to six months at a time. I would respectfully ask the government to consider whether or not it will abandon its request to carry over the billions of dollars into the next fiscal year in the borrowing authority for which it is asking, and which its majority will undoubtedly get for it. I would ask the government to be more cautious and more prudent, to spend money as though it was its own rather than as though it was somebody else's, like the proverbial drunken sailor who never knows when to stop. That is what appears to be happening now and we cannot afford it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, talking about borrowing legislation is an all too frequent duty we perform in this House. It would now seem that almost every six months we are called upon as Members of Parliament to talk about the government borrowing more money.
While I will in the time at my disposal try to criticize this particular borrowing legislation, I want to make it clear it is not my opinion that the government should take the view that it necessarily would have to cut down its social and other programs which are of service to Canadians. It is fair to say, I think, that all the programs the government has today are not necessarily of service to Canadians and there is some trimming that can take place.
More importantly, this government has taken the view that it is able to pay for what is required only by taxation and by borrowing, without taking a look at the more important aspect, the generation of wealth in Canada. The very nature of the way the government borrows increases the tax burden on all Canadians.
In this legislation the government is requesting some $14 billion in borrowing authority, but its main estimates show legitimate requirements of only $11 billion. In other words, the government is setting aside an additional $3 billion for movie money, spillage or loose change, and that is not accounted for. That is something which this opposition, combined with members of the New Democratic Party, ought to be opposing. No one should be granting any government authority to go to the market to borrow money when it has not accounted for the need for it.
This government is asking that we as the Parliament of Canada authorize it to borrow money for which it has not indicated any requirement. Why should we be asked to do that? Why should we be asked to give this government money when the people of Canada do not know whether it will be

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
used to promote the agricultural industry, industrial sales or Lord knows what? This money might be used to promote what might be, in the eyes of some, wasteful programs. The prime purpose behind the establishment of Parliament was control of the King's purse. The purpose of Parliament today is to control government expenditures, and I submit that this government has not really accounted for its expenditures in a justifiable way.
A review of the recent history of this government shows that we should be concerned about more than just today's bill, which may appear legitimate in isolation but is not. I believe in Hamlet a situation like this is described as mirrors facing mirrors-borrowing upon borrowing upon borrowing. In the last four years this government has borrowed some $40.1 billion. The projected deficits for the next four years, not counting this one, amount to an additional $51.8 billion. In other words, in the eight-year period beginning four years ago and projected four years into the future we will have borrowed some $100 billion. Canada has a population of 24 million people. A debt of $100 billion will be an albatross around the neck of Canadian society.
Today the government is asking for the authority to borrow $14 billion. It has indicated a need for only $11 billion. The government is asking for more than it requires, and it has not shown why it needs that extra money. For that reason alone the government ought not to be granted permission to borrow in the international market, because by its very nature that borrowing is a detriment to the Canadian citizen.
The truth of the matter is that of every $4 the Canadian taxpayer pays in tax, one of those dollars goes to pay interest on accumulated foreign debt. By adding another $3 billion to the required $11 billion in the main estimates as a spillage allowance just for unforeseen, unknown contingencies, the government is asking Canadian taxpayers to accept a greater tax burden. That militates against our balance of payments because it is an outflow of money. That outflow will increase taxes in our country but, more significantly, it reduces the rate of growth of wealth in the private sector of our nation. We could have all we have in this country plus more, but we must generate wealth by giving incentives to those people who use their imaginations to create.
This country is being run by a group of men and women who simply do not understand the scope and potential of the land. They do not have any understanding of money. They have the piggy-bank philosophy of people much younger than most of the people here.
During the past year the government chose to bail out Chrysler Corporation and Massey-Ferguson because they were unsuccessful, but the strongest and most successful industry in Canada at the time was the oil industry, which the government chose to nationalize. Through disincentives, the potential for some of the greatest employment and wealth opportunities not only for Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia but also Ontario, Quebec and the rest of Canada has been driven away. Two tar sands plants have been closed down because of the
inability of this government to recognize that oil is not found, as it were, in a lake underneath the ground.
Hon. members opposite do not understand the concept of a tertiary formation. They believe, falsely, that the only reason for requested oil price increases is the existence of OPEC. That is false and wrong. There are new capital costs involved in the production of oil in this country. We now have to wash rock with solvents in order to bring oil from under the ground to the surface. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has been unable to come to an agreement on price, and that inability has stopped two tar sands projects.
I want to put on the record just what projects have been stopped. Many in this country think this government has hurt only Alberta, which it has. I come from that province and I know. However, I want hon. members opposite to know that they have also hurt very seriously the province of Ontario. The people of that province need jobs. In its 25-year lifetime one tar sands plant would put $108 billion into the Ontario economy through direct expenditure. This expenditure is on iron, steel, financing, trades and services. This expenditure is on the fabrication of machinery. The list goes on and on and adds up to direct expenditures of $108 billion in the province of Ontario.
This country is one of the few which has the luxury of being able to talk about energy self-sufficiency. We have that potential. To realize it we need eight tar sands plants. Something in excess of $800 billion could have been poured into Ontario in the next 25 years, but this government has embarked on a program to stop such progress and has let the citizens of central Canada blame the province of Alberta. According to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the people of Alberta will be rich beyond our wildest imagination.
Even if there were not direct expenditures in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec as a result of the development of the potential we have, indirect spending would put more money into the pockets of people in the Atlantic region, the north, the west and other regions, and they would do with that money what anyone would do. They would spend it. People would buy automobiles made in central Canada. They would buy clothing made in Quebec or Ontario. They would buy refrigerators, toasters and other appliances made in central Canada. Eighty per cent of newly generated wealth in any region circulates through the industrial basin within six months. There is no truth to the suggestion that if the regions get richer, the centre becomes poorer. That is false thinking. This government does not need to go to the international trough to borrow money because this land has the potential to create wealth to a degree which would be unimaginable to any other nation in the world. Fish and tin are the only resources Japan has, yet it has one of the best economies in the world.
We in this country want for nothing. We have agricultural lands, mineral wealth, forests, fresh waters and oceans. With all this we can create wealth. We do not need to go to the international market.
I see, sir, that it is one o'clock. You are probably hungry, so I will continue at 2 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing I want to do on one of the loveliest days that Ottawa has experienced in some time is to thank you, sir, for coming back. Spring is here in Ottawa.
Before one o'clock we were speaking on a most serious matter, the borrowing bill, in which the government is asking Parliament for authority to enter the international markets and borrow $14 billion to maintain its programs. As outlined, and I will not dwell on it, they indicate they need some $11 billion, yet there is a request for $14 billion. In short, they are asking Parliament to underwrite $3 billion for which they have not accounted. And that, sir, as I indicated before lunch, is wrong in principle.
Equally wrong is a country like Canada having to borrow in the first place, when we have the potential for tremendous generation of wealth. If we bear in mind that our gross national debt is now $120 billion, our biggest budgetary expense is the servicing of this debt. The greatest outflow of capital from Canada is not the multinational corporations, as some would have this Parliament believe; it is not somebody coming in from outside and taking our money away. The greatest outflow of capital from Canada is the money paid to service our foreign debt. And that debt hamstrings Canadians in their attempt to achieve the standard of living they deserve.
I believe, sir, it is somewhat difficult for the public to comprehend the magnitude of these numbers. We talk about borrowing $14 billion, and in this amendment we ask that that amount be reduced to some $8 billion, thereby giving the government a portion of what they ask for but also making them more accountable to us for their borrowing requirements. To put this in perspective, I remind those Canadians who have never seen $1 billion that a $1 bill is exactly six inches long, and if you place one billion of them end to end you will have a line stretching from Vancouver to Halifax two and half times. The amount this government seeks under closure is 35 ribbons of $1 bills stretching from Vancouver to Halifax, and this after only two days of debate and analysis. That, I submit, is the second thing that is wrong.
As I was saying before, what we in this nation ought to do is look to the wealth we can create. If we look at a country such as Japan with 110 million people, its only resources are fish and tin yet it has one of the strongest economies in the world.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
The Japanese are outstripping us in the automotive and electronic markets. Now they are outstripping us in the steel industry; they are producing as much steel as North America and almost as much as the European Common Market. On this little island of Japan, people have been given the incentive to work and have been encouraged to put their industries in place. It is a land with little resource; here we are with virtually everything.
The Japanese import their uranium, coal and oil for energy; they import their wood for whatever they might build. They do this at world prices, yet they are competitive in the automotive industry. We in Canada try to guard against natural increases in the prices of world commodities. Our automotive industry bought that line. Since 1971 the government has tried to pad the cushion. Now we are paying $240 million in guaranteed loans to the Chrysler Corporation because it is not adjusting to world conditions.
Our country needs to get back to a sound basis of economics which will allow us to go forward and make changes that adjust to the new conditions of our time, instead of having government interference. Instead of promoting the entrepreneurial minds of the nation, the government becomes the stumbling block which trips up the private sector.
Our country should not have to borrow. We should be making more than we are at the present time from tax revenues. We should have a much wealthier private sector because there is no nation in the world with resources as rich as ours.
I see Mr. Speaker giving me a victory signal. I appreciate that, but I want to indicate that the philosophy of this nation is doing an untold injustice to Canadians. As a citizen of this country and as a resident of Alberta, I want to share with all that it does not make sense to pour out of our nation nearly $4 billion every year for the purchase of offshore petroleum. This gives Canadians a terrible deal.
We are buying oil from Mexico. Some people think we are purchasing it at world price, but I submit that we are not. We are purchasing it at a price which is much higher than world price. Oil is not just oil. For example, Albertan oil is some of the highest quality oil in the world. Mexican oil is a Maya oil; it is heavy oil; it is sludge oil. In truth it is junk oil. It takes 1.5 barrels to 1.6 barrels of Mexican oil to make the equivalent amount of gasoline which would come from an Alberta barrel. We are not paying $38, $40 or $42 per barrel for Mexican oil because we are only getting a portion of the amount in gasoline. It could be argued that we are paying as high as $54 per barrel because of that conversion factor.
When we get the Mexican oil here, it cannot be refined as cheaply. The federal government tries to make the citizens of Canada believe that somehow it is looking after the centre, when the fact of the matter is that it is holding Canadians back and discriminating against them in many ways.
Before the luncheon break I mentioned the two tar sands plants which have been slowed down in Alberta. They would

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
have generated wealth not only in Alberta but in Ontario as well. I should like to put on the record what one of those plants would have meant to the province of Ontario in terms of generating wealth. Out of the $108 billion in direct spending in the province of Ontario, $800 million would have been spent in iron and steel; $370 million would have been spent for metal fabrication and machinery; $325 million would have been spent for transportation equipment. I see Mr. Speaker is indicating that my time is up, but I would like to finish by saying that another $740 million would be spent in Ontario for manufacturing and processing and another $370 million for financing.
In conclusion, the country needs money, but borrowing is not the only way to get money. There are other methods; we can generate wealth within the country by encouraging our citizens. This is one of the greatest nations in the world. It has the potential, and we must excite our citizens to it. This is one of the lucky countries which has such potential.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Trade)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Trade)
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1981-82 SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not planned on taking part in this debate, but what has happened in the House in recent weeks and the repeated delays responsible for the fact that we are only now studying a bill which should normally have been passed several days ago, have perhaps made me more aware of the issue concerning the borrowing authority of the government and the related question of successive budgetary deficits of the Canadian government.
No one likes deficits, Mr. Speaker. I am convinced that the Minister of Finance, or rather the Minister of State responsible for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) dislikes deficits as much as the financial manager of a big company or even the couple who, on going over its budget at the end of the month, realizes that it is in the red for a few dollars and will have to borrow money from the bank or another source.
However, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that this estimated deficit of $11 billion, which does not take into account any contingencies, has to be financed. This is necessary if we do not want or are not able to eliminate it completely. And when I speak of eliminating it completely, I mean immediately since the cash requirements of the government aim at meeting commitments that the House accepted in the past and has asked the government to see to it by administering certain programs. Unless we cut back drastically on these programs, the government needs sufficient funds to pay for them. The dilemna which we must therefore face, and this is the reason for today's debate, is that either we have the necessary amount in the treasury or else we do not have it. For the moment, we do not have it!
The second dilemma would be as follows; Either we administer the programs approved by the House itself in the past, or else we cut back on these programs. That is the second dilemma.
What are the facts finally? The facts are as follows: Considering the estimated revenue for the current fiscal year, we have additional cash requirements of $11 billion. Second, because of a certain number of contingencies in the Canadian economy, it might be possible and even desirable that these cash requirements be increased, and the government has provided for this purpose an additional borrowing authority of $3 billion. The government hopes that it will need less, but it could eventually need more. Let us suppose, for instance, that the world oil prices increase and that the compensation offered by the Canadian government increases proportionately. The reserve would melt away like snow in the sun.
These are the facts. The only thing that the government wants to do with this bill is not to approve or reapprove the programs already approved by this House, it is not to obtain a blank cheque to do as it pleases without taking into account any need to reassess some of the existing programs. Not at all! The only thing that the government is doing is to ask the House to provide the necessary funds to administer these programs.
If we, the members of this House, believe that some of these programs should be re-evaluated, that is fine. We only have to make suggestions. The opposition has during every session a number of allotted days during which it can suggest cutbacks to certain programs or any other action that it would like the government to take, and these issues are discussed and eventually voted on. This is the proper way to proceed.
Although some people say it is not enough, in its budget tabled last November the government itself set up a contingency plan in an effort to curb rising government expenditures. That is another possible and regular avenue since the government presents its budget and the House deals with it through the votes taken after the budget debate. But that is not what we are doing today, Mr. Speaker. The only thing we are doing today through this bill is simply to authorize the government to administer its programs and to have the funds to do so.
In the present conditions I find it somewhat difficult to understand why the opposition should be so dead set against this provision. I can see why a certain number of members would rise on both sides of the House to deplore the deficit and increasing government expenditures; that is normal and it is our duty; it is normal as well in the end that distress signals be flashed to spur the government into doing more to put the lid on its expenses, and I accept that. But when they resort to a filibuster to prevent the adoption of a measure which in the end will do nothing more than release funds or authorize borrowing so that the government will be able to administer the programs which we ourselves have adopted, I fail to see there anything so improper that they would force the government to invoke closure. I know that members opposite screamed themselves hoarse, as they are wont to do, when they heard we would bring in closure or time allocation for this measure. It is normal that the opposition should criticize when

a time allocation is slapped on a legislative measure. Indeed, I for one must admit that as a member I am always a bit reluctant every time I have to vote on such a motion. That is normal, I am a parliamentarian. On the other hand I sit on the government benches and I must always weigh the interests involved.
But in this case, Mr. Speaker, we are not dealing at all with a legislative measure which forces new programs upon the people, nor is it a legislative measure which will give the government a mandate to spend more than expected. It is nothing more than a piece of legislation which will enable the government-and I am saying this for the nth time-to administer programs that we have been approved in the House. Under the circumstances, once the distress signals have been sent out, once the deficit has been deplored and the government has been urged to get a handle on the deficit, we have no choice but to take the necessary steps to fulfil those wishes ourselves in the House. Earlier I suggested two ways to go about it, but in the meantime the government must have a free hand to administer those programs. It cannot administer without money.
Our financial requirements for 1981-82 amount to $11 billion. Members across the aisle have complained because the bill under study provides an additional $3 billion as a reserve. A number of speakers have explained why the government is seeking the approval of the House to borrow an additional $3 billion. Personally, I think that it is very wise on the part of the government to make sure in advance that it will be able to cope with unforeseen contingencies which might crop up, and experience has shown that year in and year out there are urgent situations in which we must act.
Besides, I remind my hon. colleagues that the bill in question also provides that, should the amounts required by the government to finance its programs by any chance not reach the $3 billion involved here, the carryover to the next year would be reduced or limited to the $3 billion requested as a reserve. So, there is no danger, as far as the House is concerned, that the government be given a blank cheque to spend as much as it wants, whether it be four, five or six billion dollars in the following year that would not have been approved here. The maximum amount is set at $3 million regardless of what amounts the government might need.
Under the circumstances, I find even more difficult to understand that some hon. members should have suggested that the government be given an amount of only four or five billion dollars, some even spoke of eight billion dollars, to face estimated expenditures of some $11 billion. I fail to understand the rationale behind that proposal. That the hon. members should suggest the use of parliamentary or administrative procedures to eliminate our deficit, I could understand, but the debate in progress in the House at this point has nothing to do with that. The bill before us only provides the government with the amounts requested.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
May I be allowed to digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker: when there is a deficit as large as it is now-and under our Constitution the Canadian government is responsible, in the final analysis, for fiscal and monetary policies-and when we see that provincial entities, our provincial partners and their administrations, including municipal administrations, represent over 60 per cent of all government expenditures in Canada, I wonder whether it might not be timely to re-examine seriously the traditional mechanisms for formulating both fiscal and monetary policies.
I know that, traditionally, the Minister of Finance plans his policies together with his advisers on the basis of economic requirements at a given time, and that nothing is supposed to transpire from those discussions, deliberations, cogitations, until eight o'clock on the night when he brings down his budget. I also remember that a minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien) innovated when time came for him to bring down his budget; I believe it was in 1977, and he consulted his provincial counterparts.
Unfortunately, the results were not exactly what had been hoped for: some wrangling followed those consultations, but that is another story. The fact remains that, to my mind, it would be advisable to give serious thought to the process by which the fiscal and monetary policies are implemented with a view to having greater input from the provinces as partners, who represent, if only as far as budgetary matters are concerned, an element of prime importance in government spending in Canada, and whose impact on the economy and interprovincial trade is such that they cannot be ignored when government policies are formulated.
How should we go about it? I think that at the institutional level, we may not have at present the necessary machinery to set up that kind of consultations. Several proposals have been made by various groups to the effect that the Canadian Parliament make of an institution of either House, probably the Upper House or an altered Upper House, a forum where provincial governments could be heard on fiscal and monetary matters.
Such a huge deficit makes you ponder, and I suggest to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance that they make overtures to their provincial counterparts, urging them to take a more active part at the consultation and concentration levels, and even perhaps at the decision-making level eventually, in drawing up the fiscal and monetary policies. My comments are perhaps somewhat irrelevant, but since you have allowed other members to stray from the subject, I think you will allow me a last digression.
The last point I should like to emphasize about this measure relates to the so-called draining of funds-that is the allegation made by some hon. members of the opposition-from the capital market in Canada. On March 20 last, the Minister of State for Finance gave some figures which clearly showed-

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 and I think one had to be blind to ignore them-that the capital market is healthy, thank you, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of such borrowings by the Government of Canada and of provincial and municipal governments, and even by all three levels of government, private financing in Canada has increased considerably in the last few years, on the bond market and on the stock market. I am not concerned about that so-called draining of funds. For the next 20 years, until the year 2000, investments of $500 million have been mentioned in the energy industry alone to develop our energy potential.
I am simply trying to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the additional $3 billion requested by the Government of Canada are not going to change the general picture very much. And as for the distress signals sent by the Progressive Conservative members regarding this so-called draining of funds, I am still waiting to hear them from the main economic agents which should normally be the first to complain about this borrowing authority given to the Government of Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, if there are problems of a philosophical, methodological or organizational nature with governmental programs, let us discuss them. Let there be proposals to abolish a number of them, to reduce, amend or review some others, But such is not the purpose of this bill. The purpose of this bill is to provide the government with the tools it needs to administer the country. So let us allow it to run the country, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some comments on this borrowing authority bill. First, we should take a look at why we are in this mess. Why do we have such a debt? Why are we borrowing so much money? Actually, it is the direct responsibility of successive Liberal governments. This goes back to 1968 when it rammed through the House under closure a measure to remove proper control and examination of government expenditures. Since then we have lost all control. Its only solution to any problem is either to print and spend more money, or to borrow more money. This has nothing to do with the Conservative Party; we opposed that measure in 1968.
I have listened to these Liberal members say that we should simply rubber stamp this measure, but I cannot accept that because I have not received any mail or communication from any of my constituents or anyone in the Greater Winnipeg area or Manitoba area which shows support for anything that this government is doing. Therefore, we are fully justified in criticizing the government, and it is legitimate criticism. The actions of the government over the years have put us into this mess. It is not something which it inherited or which simply happened.
I suggest that more of government members should read the Auditor General's report and the Lambert Commission report, and then they would understand what I am talking about. The
previous Liberal speaker said that some of the provinces are in debt too, that they are borrowing, and perhaps we should meet with them to discuss mutual problems. We had that in mind, and the Conservative government had an item on the agenda of the First ministers' conference on December 15, 1979-that is, two days after it was defeated-to discuss duplication between the provincial and federal governments. That would have been a real and genuine start to eliminate duplication between the two levels of government. I am sure that would have saved untold millions. However, I do not see any suggestions from this government about getting together with the provinces or anyone else to discuss reducing expenditures or finding ways of eliminating duplication and waste.
Another reason we are borrowing, that so much money is going out of the country and we are in such a mess with our energy policy, is that another program which was introduced by the Diefenbaker government in the early 1960s, a road to resources program to develop all our resources in the north, was discontinued. At that time the Liberal opposition laughed at it, and when the Liberal government took office again in 1963 it dropped the road to resources program to develop the north. We could very well have been self-sufficient today if that program had been continued, and the Liberal Party would have received most of the credit. However, the program was dropped. That is why we are in such a mess. Billions of dollars are going out of Canada, to OPEC countries to buy imported oil, and this is another reason we are in debt and borrowing more money.
We are quite justified in our criticism if we read the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other hon. members of the government since 1968 to the effect that they would bring expenditures under control, that if they did not bring them under control we would have inflation. Those have been meaningless, empty words. They have done nothing to bring anything under control at all. UIC payments are increasing, which will be another burden on taxpayers. Perhaps many taxpayers do not fully understand what is meant when we talk of expenditures and estimates. Perhaps they believe such expenditure do not affect them, but they certainly do. We are talking about the money of these taxpayers, and they are the ones who must pay all the interest charges and pay for all the reckless spending.
Another example of spending is the metric conversion program which is now going through and will hit the retail food industry so hard. Scales will have to be purchased from outside of this country at a cost of $50 million, and that will be another burden on the Canadian taxpayer and will drive food costs way up. The government is simply ramming that program through, also by order in council, as another example of its contempt for the Canadian people.
I would like to run through the 1981-82 main estimates. This is an overview of overspending. I would like to point out that Conservative Members of Parliament were banned from the briefing on these estimates, and we did not appreciate that. When one examines the government's spending plans for the
April 3, 1981

next year, it is not hard to see why it wanted to minimize the ability of the opposition to respond quickly in the House.
The total spending forecast for next year is $67.6 billion. That is an increase of 12.8 per cent. So where is the control? Where is the restraint which is always talked about during election times? This is breaking the Liberal commitment to hold spending increases to less than the GNP growth, which is forecast to be 11.3 per cent in the coming year. The forecast of $67.6 billion is achieved only through some juggling of accounts. For example, $2.4 billion of petroleum compensation fund expenditures no longer appears as an expense, as it is now being netted out against the petroleum products levy.
The Liberals will spend $3.8 billion more next year than the Conservative government had planned to spend. That is a legitimate complaint from our side. We do not believe that that is necessary at all. It is a question of philosophy. The socialists love to spend and they love uncontrolled growth in government. I will go into that in a little more detail in a moment.
Government spending next year is equal to the sum of money needed to purchase a $75,000 home for every household in the province of British Columbia. In spite of reports by the Auditor General that the public service is operating at only 60 per cent efficiency, and in spite of commitments made last April by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) that he would take steps to reduce the size of the public service, there will be a net increase of 3,085 person-years next year. We hear repeated statements that we must control growth of the civil service. They are just meaningless, empty and hollow words.
Things could be worse than that, Mr. Speaker. However, the net figure is based on the assumption that the post office will have a net reduction of 461 person-years as a result of expected efficiency gains in postal operations. The public debt charges constitute the fastest growing envelope, rising by $2.1 billion as a consequence of higher debt and higher interest rates.
My colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), illustrated what a billion dollars means. Many Canadians think that the expenditure of billions of dollars does not concern them. I want to assure the people of Canada that what is contained in those billions of dollars is their hard-earned tax dollars. It is not someone else's money. No one else is giving us money. Canadians are paying for these billions of dollars being borrowed, billions of dollars of uncontrolled spending and debt charges.
The estimates show that while planned spending for this year has not changed since last fall's budget, there has been a change in the composition of the expenditure envelopes. Significantly, instead of spending $7,155 million on economic development as projected, the government will only spend $6,873 million. At least half of the cut will go to pay for the increase in the cost of services to the government.

The estimated cost of services to government was $4 billion in 1980-1981. The fall budget projected the cost at $4.5 billion. This figure has again been revised upward to $4.7 billion; in other words, a 17 per cent increase. Only a Liberal government would consider a significant increase in the cost of its overheads when faced with near bankruptcy. That is why so many hon. members are debating this bill and exposing these people.
In spite of a 50 per cent increase in UIC premiums this year, the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance account is up by $219 million.
The federal government treats national unity the way most people treat the weather; they like to talk about it. The cost of talking about it will rise by $11 million next year, all for increased information by way of advertising. The government might as well cancel the advertising because it is having absolutely no effect on the Canadian public, either in regard to the constitutional package or anything else. It is just a waste of money.
Another area we discuss time and time again, an area that we took some efforts to bring under control when we formed the government, is that of cost overruns. If this government were bringing cost overruns under control, perhaps we would not have so many speakers being so critical. But cost overruns are continuing and the figures are astronomical. There were 497 projects with cost overruns of over $1 billion. This information was released by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). The average overrun was about $10 million. One of the worst departments for cost overruns is the Department of the Environment. Of 223 projects, 153 experienced cost overruns, at a total cost of $283 million. Another example of a cost overrun is the Lachine canal in the amount of $45.9 million. What kind of management do we have from these people if we have overruns to this extent?
One of the largest overruns in dollar terms was in the Department of National Defence, with $98.7 million for the Aurora patrol aircraft. This was almost a 900 per cent cost overrun compared to the original budget. What is going on in national defence to cause a 900 per cent cost overrun? I asked the minister the same question in the House. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) could give no explanation for this. He did not even seem to be concerned when asked. When we formed the government we set up a committee to investigate cost overruns, but since the Liberals now form the government they feel this work is best done in the public accounts committee.
Another measure we took when we were the government to try to control overruns was to introduce a measure called "double jeopardy." This measure of double jeopardy penalized departments $2 for every $1 overrun. I imagine that measure has been dropped by this government.
Another area where there does not seem to be any control is the number of Crown corporations we have in Canada today. We have approximately 436 Crown corporations. Why on earth does Canada need 436 Crown corporations? In 1962

there were 35 Crown corporations. That figure is up to 400 plus today.
Prior to the Conservatives taking over as the government, we tried to find out in committee how many Crown corporations there were. The government could not even tell us how many Crown corporations there were, but we ferreted the information out in the committee. It took us a few weeks and I see some of the members who were involved in that process are here today. The officials told us that the figure was around 100 Crown corporations. By contrast, when we formed the government one of our priorities was to rationalize the functions and purposes of these corporations as well as to bring them under a scheme of financial accountability. Using the recommendations of the Lambert commission as a basis, the Conservative government introduced Bill C-27 to increase the accountability of and control over Crown corporations. I received a document in my office this week on accountable management. It is a progress report to Parliament from the President of the Treasury Board. I see Crown corporations are included in this document. Let us hope that this is a genuine report and that the government is making a genuine effort to control the growth of Crown corporations and make them more accountable.
One example brought to my attention recently concerned the CBC. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is talking about establishing CBC-2. The CBC has been before the CRTC with an application, but it did not get very far. Questions have been raised in the House as to whether the government supports CBC-2. The government has not said too much as to whether or not it is committed to the formation of CBC-2. I have information that the CBC is spending money developing logos and new tapes for CBC-2. The government should be questioning the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to find out why that money is being spent on CBC-2 when the CBC does not even have the permission of the CRTC, the cabinet or of anybody else to develop that channel. I hope the government will be making a statement about this matter very soon or I shall continue my own investigation.

Mr. Speaker, I have always participated in some stage of a borrowing authority debate, and this is the second opportunity I have had with regard to this bill. I would like to go over some of the problems this borrowing bill creates and the reasons for those problems. The borrowing bill does not present a totally bad picture; some parts of it are quite favourable.
When we talk about debt and how much we have to borrow because of the national debt, we must do so in terms of assets and income. I wish to cite an example which I have cited before. If I owed $10,000 and my income was $100,000 a year, there would be a relationship between my income and that debt. If I owed $10,000 and my income was $20,000 a year 1 would be talking about a different ratio. The amount of debt
April 3, 1981

would be the same, but my ability to pay would be very different. The same is true with assets. If my assets were ten or 20 times the amount of debt I owe, I would be in good shape. However, if my assets were very small compared to the amount I owe, I would be in bad shape, even though the amount owed would be the same.
The same is true at the federal level. We cannot speak of a $10 billion debt 20 years ago and a $70 billion or $80 billion debt today and say it is a terrible situation, that we are much worse off now. That is not quite true. In 1951 the net national debt as a portion of the gross national product was approximately 51 per cent. In other words, the federal debt that year was 50 per cent of the gross national product. After the Korean war, that figure came down. By 1962 it was something like 32 or 33 per cent. Last year, without getting into a lot of detail, it was in the order of 30 per cent.
One can say that we are better off today in terms of the relationship of debt to revenue than in 1951. When talking about these figures, one must talk in terms of revenues and GNP. It is foolish to talk about them in any other fashion.
If we look at government expenditures, we see that 68 per cent of the total is by way of transfers to provinces and municipalities through various and sundry subsidies. Of the remaining 32 per cent, 27.7 per cent is for the operation of the government and 4 per cent is used for subsidies to Crown corporations. Added together, the total operation of the government is something in the area of 32 per cent of all expenditures.
The opposition keeps talking about cutting expenditures and reducing the deficit. What bothers me most is that they want all of that reduction from the 32 per cent. They say it is absolutely essential to cut back on government expenditures, the number of civil servants, salaries of civil servants and government waste. That will not solve the problem. There may be some fat, there probably is, and we may be able to cut that back by 10 or 15 per cent; but to really do something about a $16 billion deficit, you have to do something very significant in the area of transfer payments.
If we are going to cut back, it must from the 68 per cent. It is fine to argue that we must cut back and reduce the deficit, but where are we to make the cutbacks? Is it to be in transfer payments to provinces, most of which is spent on medical and hospital care or those on welfare? Should we cut back on unemployment insurance payments?
I had some discussions yesterday regarding a significant cut by provincial and federal governments in educational grants to young adults who do not have a decent education. Are we going to cut back in that area? That may make sense to some people, but if we cut back in that area, I can assure you that for the next 40 years those people who are not going to have this educational opportunity will be the ones on the welfare, UIC rolls, and so on. If we cut back in that area, will we really be doing something?
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
I can remember talk about cutting back in the province of Ontario, particularly in medical expenses, and cutbacks in areas like halfway houses for people with mental health problems. We may save $30 a day in this way, but then we have to pay $200 a day to keep the same person in an institution later on in life.
When we talk about cutting, we also have to talk about which cuts make sense and which do not. I would make a wager that every one of us in this House has half a dozen things we would never want to see cut back. I do not want to see cutbacks in those educational grants for young adults who have, for some reason or other, not acquired an adequate education to function properly. Other members have other special interest areas such as medicare. Some suggest we need more police, more prisons and we have to tighten up our laws. Where do we cut? If we cut what you want maintained, it may have something to do with the law, and if we cut what I want maintained, it may have something to do with the future of young people.
It is very easy for the opposition to say we have to cut back, but it is not easy when you have to sit down and decide what are the cuts you want. Let the opposition tell us the things they want cut, those things that are significant.
Do not tell me we are going to solve the deficit problem by making cuts in the public service. I can tell you this represents only 32 per cent of total government expenditure. It is a good portion, but if there are to be cuts, they will have to be made in that other 68 per cent or we will have to increase our revenues to make up the difference.
I know we all come to the cutting stage as members of this House, and we come to that stage every day. Someone thinks something should be cut and some of us say: My God, that cannot happen because it is important that this money be supplied. All I ever hear from the other side is that we have to cut back, but I have yet to hear what they want us to cut back. It seems to me we all face the same problem. We have good programs. For one reason or another I think a specific program is good. For example, I think housing programs for native people are good programs, and I can think of all kinds of other things we have to do which are important. Either we do these intelligent things or we ignore all kinds of segments of our society which are weaker or for some reason cannot manage.
Either we cut back, or we start talking about how we raise revenues. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) talks about tax expenditures, I think this is an approach which has to be looked at. Whether or not that is the approach we will take, or the approach you would take, is immaterial, but in some way we have to begin considering revenues.
There is another notion I would like to deal with in the next few minutes which has to do with this whole business of big government, government revenues and expenditures. Let me give you some idea of what has happened since World War II in terms of government revenue. These figures again relate to

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 gross national product. There is no point in saying we had a certain revenue in 1951 and today it is five times that much. That does not mean anything. What is important is how much is our gross national product and how that figure relates to revenues. That is what is important.
I should like to look at provincial and federal revenues, and, if we want, we could add municipal revenues. For the moment let us just consider federal and provincial revenue.
In 1943, and this was in wartime, 22.3 per cent of the gross national product of the country went in revenue to the federal government. In the same year, 3.3 per cent of the gross national product of the country went to all the provinces. By 1955, the percentage of the gross national product in these terms had dropped to 17.6 per cent, while the provincial share had gone up to 4.8 per cent. I am referring to the percentage of the gross national product.
These figures are taken for every five years, so I am not picking out odd years. In 1960, the federal portion of the gross national product in terms of revenue was 17.0 per cent and the provinces' share was 6.1 per cent. In 1965, the federal share had dropped to 16.4 per cent and the provincial share had gone up to 8.9 per cent. In 1970, the federal share was 16.1 per cent and the provincial share was 12.3 per cent. In 1975, the federal share was 19.2 per cent and the provincial share was 13.5 per cent.
The last year for which I have figures is 1979, so there is only a four-year gap there. The federal share had slipped back to 16 per cent of gross national product and the provincial share was 15 per cent. The provincial percentage had increased by about 500 per cent, from between 3 per cent and 4 per cent to about 15 per cent of gross national product, while the federal share had gone from 22.3 per cent to 16 per cent.
Everyone always talks about the federal government as being the cause of inflation and of everything else, but is it this government that is to blame? If it is to be blamed, then we on this side have to accept that blame because for all but about six or seven years of that period we were in power.
Let us get away from war years and not even consider those. Let us move to 1955 when we were out of both wars, nicely away from them. In that year, the percentage was 17.6 per cent federal versus 4.8 per cent provincial, or about four times as much. Let us go back to 1979, 24 years later, when we find that the federal share was down to 16 per cent from 17.6 per cent, whereas the provinces' share had one up to 15.0 per cent.
When we are talking about the borrowings of the government, government debt, and so on, we have to look at the areas of government spending. We are now talking about 1980-82. In this period of time the federal government will transfer in terms of tax transfers and direct transfers something like $18.8 billion to provincial revenues. That is something in the order of 23 per cent or 24 per cent of all government spending. Let me have a look at those transfers because I think they are tremendously important.
I must say something about the nonsense that has been said in this House, particularly by the Tory party, about the
Constitution. The real constitutional story relates to how we are to face this tremendous transfer to the provinces; how we are to deal with it in the next few years.
I will talk about that a little more a little later on, but I would like to talk first about the kinds of things on which we actually do transfer funds to the provinces. I said the amount was $18.88 billion, but basically it is $18.9 billion out of $67 billion. That money goes to things like hospital insurance, which amounts to $2.9 billion. These are rounded-off figures. Medicare gets $1 billion; post-secondary education, close to $2 billion; extended health care, another $700 million; and so forth. The Canada Assistance Plan gets $2 billion to assist the provinces to pay welfare. Federal money is transferred to a whole series of these kinds of things. The amount transferred for bilingualism comes to something less than $200 million. It is not the major factor many Canadians think it is. The amounts spent on all these things total a very substantial transfer from the federal government to the provinces and other levels of government. I think this is a fundamental matter we must consider.
