I want to open my remarks with just a few comments on the remarks of the previous speaker, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae), who uses figures in an attempt to establish the position that somehow the federal government in this country is not large enough yet and that it must become much, much larger because the provinces have, relatively speaking, closed the gap in terms of the difference-at least as measured on an expenditure scale- in power between the federal government and the provinces. What the hon. member has neglected to do is to examine the data he has put forward. Instead, he has taken the figures which have been produced by the propagandists in the federal-
April 3, 1981

provincial office in an attempt to justify this constitutional coup d'etat.
If the hon. member examined the figures put out, he would realize that the description of what constitutes the federal government's proportion of the gross national product omits a considerable amount of federal government activity. For example, those Figures are based on the spending estimates as defined in our estimates, which are not the federal government's spending in total by any stretch of the imagination. The blue book estimates describe only those expenditures which go through the consolidated revenue fund and, as I intend to show in a few minutes, that is not the total government spending by any stretch of the imagination. The numbers the hon. member talked about do not account for expenditures by the some 436 Crown corporations which are wholly owned by the federal government. They do not account for the separate government operations which do not go through the consolidated revenue fund, such as UIC, the Canada Pension Plan or the oil import compensation plan, all of which amount to another $7 billion or $8 billion which should be added to the figures about which the hon. member spoke.
If the hon. member looked at the real figures, and not those figures cooked up by Dr. Goebbels' workers over the unity information office, he would find that, in fact, there is not a case to be made that somehow this federal government has had its power reduced to such an insignificant level in this country that it should beat off those terrible, voracious provinces which are trying to usurp the power which rightfully belongs to the federal government. The facts simply do not substantiate that argument, if we look at the real facts and not just those produced by those propagandists the federal government employs as part of its campaign on the Constitution.
Bill C-59, and the amendment thereto which we are discussing at the report stage, is one of those bills which can be defined very simply. It contains just a few clauses. It is one of those simple bills with just a few clauses which, as usual, are the most profound in terms of their impact. What the government is asking for is authority to borrow $14 billion. That is a colossal amount of money. A billion is beyond my capability to imagine. My colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), mentioned that a billion minutes ago Jesus Christ was walking on the earth. We are talking about $14 billion which the government wants to borrow. The government needs this money, we are told, because it has run out of authority. We are already into debt to the tune of $140 billion. Hon. members opposite need more money with which to operate the government because spending is simply out of control. The borrowing of this $14 billion will just cover, with a little extra, the interest on the debt which has been accumulated by this government over the last few years. This $14 billion will not be used for all those nice programs about which the previous speaker spoke. This $14 billion will not be used to assist old age pensioners, to assist native Canadians or to assist other people in this country with their problems. The $14 billion we will be authorizing the government to borrow will be used to pay the interest on previous borrowing. We will be borrowing
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82 $14 billion to pay the interest on the accumulated debt of previous years. Next year we will have to borrow that much more to pay the ongoing interest plus the interest on this $14 billion, which will be another couple billion at least. And on and on we go on this upside down pyramid. It is an atrocious situation.
As citizens, Mr. Speaker, you or I cannot operate our own personal finances that way. No one would lend us the money if we attempted to operate our finances that way. If we tried to borrow more money simply to cover the carrying costs of what we had borrowed before, no one would lend it to us. No company can do that. No family can do that. No provincial government can do that, as a matter of fact. The only institution which can do that is the federal government because it has something no one else has. It has a printing press which can print money. The government owns the money presses. It has the central bank. The federal government is the only one which can get away with this, and even the federal government can get away with it only for a while because even central governments in large, rich countries like Canada at some point in time are faced with the same kinds of realities faced by individuals, institutions, corporations or anyone else in the world.
The previous speaker talked about the marvellous ways in which government can spend money, and there is no denying that. He says it is easier to spend than to cut or save. Well, that is hardly an argument. Everybody recognizes that, of course, it is easier to spend than to cut, and there are all kinds of worth-while things the government should be doing. There is not a member in this House who could not dream up 10, 20, 30 or 100 new spending programs which would have a very beneficial impact. So there is no question that there is a demand, very worth-while in many instances, on government for new programs. There is no question that a civilized government and Parliament, consisting of people genuinely concerned about their country and fellow citizens, must look at the possibility of coming to the assistance of those in our society who need it. We have to be concerned about health care, about education and about our senior citizens. We have to look after them; there is no argument on that.
So, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member arguing that point was arguing with a strawman. However, on the other side, there must be recognition by government that these programs have to be financed from taxes. There is no such thing as a free lunch; somebody has to pay, and I humbly submit that the people of Canada are more than ready to pay the taxes to look after our senior citizens. I have no doubt that Canadians are more than willing to pay for adequate health services and adequate education, and to pay those taxes necessary to fund programs which they approve of. Where we get into trouble, Mr. Speaker-and this government has habitually been in this phase since 1968-is where the government wants to undertake programs of benefit to Canadians but does not want to take the responsibility for saying: you will have to pay for it. They do not want to admit that taxes have to be raised, so they

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
pretend that is a separate function and they do it in a number of ways.
One of the ways of doing that is running up deficits, because while they have to be paid off eventually, they are paid off by the next generation five, ten, 20 years from now. And in ten years, when some members are standing up here complaining about the accumulated debt, we could stand up and say: a lot of this is the fault of Mr. Pearson; and it is his fault, but who cares? He is gone, there is no political fault.
So members of this government recognize they can introduce programs today, get the political benefit and then let future generations pay for them because by then they will be gone to their just rewards as directors, or as presidents, or chairmen of Crown corporations, and they do not have to worry about it. So there is the irresponsibility of their approach.
The other way they do it, Mr. Speaker, and this offends me perhaps more than anything else, is by disguising the actual level of spending. They are not honest about what they are spending. They do this in a lot of ways. To begin with, the government, this one in particular in the last few years, has never told the Canadian public honestly what it is spending in its estimates. For example, when the main estimates were brought down this year, there was a press lock up. No experts were allowed, no members of the opposition, only working members of the press gallery were allowed in. They were given prepared press releases by the government which carried this message. They were kept locked up until the House opened for business, and then they ran off and announced to the Canadian public that government spending was 12.8 per cent.

speechtext: While you ran a filibuster.

Well, Mr. Speaker, the next day, when the experts had a chance to look at the figures, when people not quite as gullible perhaps as members of the media-and I should not fault them because they are under pressure of time and have to produce their stories-they found that spending had gone up 16 per cent, not 12.8 per cent. But the story had gone out; the public had been told by the government it was 12.8 per cent. The real figure of 16 per cent went out in a few columns. Don McGillivray of Southam's brought it to the attention of those who read the business pages of which are not many. There were a few Canadians who saw the truth and pointed it out, but the vast majority of Canadians still believe the original figure put out by the government. They were able to get that figure before the public because of blatant manipulation of the media, by having that lock up and not allowing in there members of the opposition and experts to examine and cross-examine the Treasury Board officials who were there.
Another way they disguise the spending, Mr. Speaker, is through the supplementary estimates. Again, across this country the figure went out that spending this year is 12.8 per cent above last year. That is a false figure. The correct figure is 16 per cent. But in addition, that is a comparison of the main estimates with the total spending of last year as shown in the main and supplementary estimates A, B and C. We know
there will be at least three more sets of supplementary estimates this year and we know that the year to year comparison, even using the cooked books, is going to be in excess of the 12.8 per cent for sure, and well in excess of 16 per cent. In fact, spending year over year, based on past experience, will likely be of the order of an 18 per cent increase. All the while, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will say: we are keeping our campaign promises of keeping government spending within the trend line of the growth in the economy. That is the kind of chicanery and downright dishonesty that goes on in terms of disguising spending.
Another way they disguise spending, Mr. Speaker, is through Crown corporations. If the government borrows money directly to undertake a program, that shows up in spending. So what they do instead is to create a Crown corporation, guarantee its loans, which is the same as if the government had borrowed the money. It never shows up in government spending and they can claim: gee, look, we are keeping spending under control. In the process, you end up with another Crown corporation, a lot more government spending and a minister who can say with a straight face, "we are under restraint; we are keeping spending under control", which is a blatant falsehood.
Another way in which they disguise the true spending is the creation of revolving funds which operate outside of the consolidated revenue fund and therefore do not show up in the blue book estimates as government spending. For example, the petroleum compensation fund whereby they subsidize some imports, is a fund separate from the blue book procedure and that money does not show up in government spending. There is also the UIC revolving fund, the airport revolving fund, and I do not know how many others. This is money being collected and spent by the government, but it never shows up in government spending so that they can continue to claim: we are holding expenditures under control, we are operating under constraint. A blatant falsehood.
Even more offensive than that, Mr. Speaker, is the use in the estimates of negative expenditures, if you can imagine that. A couple of years ago, when they had a desire, for political reasons, to claim that they were holding government spending under control, they had CMHC sell some mortgages. In other words, they sold some capital. They did not list the receipts of those sales as an income item; they listed them as a negative expenditure to keep the expenditures down. It was the kind of book-cooking for which individuals in the private sector would end up in court.
In this year's main estimates of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, there is a negative expenditure, under the petroleum compensation fund, of 52,665,400,000. It was a negative expenditure, because they raised more money than they spent in that revolving fund. Rather than taking the honest approach and listing it on the revenue side of the
April 3, 1981

ledger, they have taken the dishonest approach and described it as a negative expenditure.
There is another manner in which government spending is hidden. Who knows what dollars are involved? It is very difficult to identify. I am referring to the government's increasing propensity to push expenditures onto the private sector. If they want a certain task undertaken, if they want a certain program or some particular action which may have some social benefit implemented, rather than paying for it directly through the government consolidated revenue fund, which would show up in their expenditure plan, they pass a law requiring the private sector to undertake that expenditure. It never shows up as a government expenditure item, but in fact it is spending for a government cause. Therefore, it is in exactly the same category as any other type of spending.
One estimate of the consulting group in Ottawa showed that the spending under this item alone could be in the order of $15 billion. If we are to bring spending and deficits under control, first and foremost, honesty is necessary. First and foremost, the government must stop disguising what it is doing. It must stop trying to fool the people. It must draw a direct relationship between spending and raising funds. It must be honest and open about the process. Then perhaps we would have a better selection of programs which should be funded. Certainly we would have better control over the government spending process, and we would not be called upon year after year to authorize untold billions of dollars of new debt.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to follow the colourful hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). Certainly I would like to pick up where he left off and raise some of the problematic sides of Bill C-59 which is before us. It is a request to borrow $14 billion. This immediately poses some very, very interesting questions.
First, when we look at the estimates, we find that $11 billion is all that is actually required. So this raises the following questions: how will the $3 billion be spent; is it a slush fund; is it simply there in case it is required somewhere down the road?
When we look at the account of the government, we find that it has $4.8 billion in the bank. This really raises the question: is it necessary at this point for the government to receive authority to borrow $14 billion? The amendment of the Tory party which recognizes the more reasonable figure of $8 billion is something we feel encouraged to support. Perhaps it is somewhat simplistic in approaching this very serious and problematic situation but, nevertheless, it is a step in the right direction.
In the short time remaining, I want to focus on four problems in terms of this request to borrow $14 billion. My concern is primarily with small businessmen, the small entrepreneurs in Canada, and what this request means to those individuals who are out there in the corner stores, the service stations, the small pharmacies, the small plants and manufacturing centres. What does this mean to these people?
First, we must recognize that the government will have to go to the domestic capital markets in order to borrow $14 billion.
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
This will have an immediate effect of increasing interest rates. It is the type of thing which jacks up interest rates and encourages higher rates than ever. Of course, higher interest rates for small businessmen mean increased carrying charges. Certainly this reduces the ability of small businessmen to compete effectively with larger corporations and companies of regional, national or even multinational spheres of influence. For example, it reduces the amount of inventory small businessmen can maintain. Therefore, it reduces the level of service they are able to provide. It adds prices to his products which makes competition very, very difficult. Needless to say, it reduces the ability of small entrepreneurs to expand their operations, to develop new product lines, or to develop new entrepreneurial activities. In a sense, it makes it very difficult for small businessmen or women to operate in a competitive fashion with larger companies, particularly those with larger spheres of influence.
When the government goes out to borrow $14 billion from the domestic capital markets, we must recognize that this in turn has a negative impact upon the medium and small business community. If the Canadian government is borrowing $14 billion from the domestic capital markets, it is $14 billion which is not being used by investors in the private sector to expand its operations. It hinders productivity, development and expansion of our economic, industrial and manufacturing sectors.
Another problem is that the government cannot borrow $14 billion from the domestic capital markets because it will jack up interest rates beyond an acceptable level. Thus, the government is forced to sell bonds and treasury bills to the Bank of Canada which increases the money supply. As the hon. member for Calgary Centre indicated, the government has the ability to print money. The printing presses come out, and the money is printed; it leads into an inflationary spiral. If there is one fear of the small businessman today, it is the fear of inflation, the inability to plan accurately for the future, and the further erosion of his small profit margin.
If the government goes beyond domestic capital markets to borrow money abroad, the possibility of very serious problems develops. For example, if there is a reduction in the value of the Canadian dollar, it is forced to repay those loans at inflated levels. In my own experience as an alderman in a western municipality, I felt that we could make a better deal if we borrowed in Swiss francs, only to see a reduction in the value of the Canadian dollar and those borrowings being paid back in deflated dollars. This is the type of situation with which the government will be faced, if it continues to borrow money abroad or from foreign markets.
The government is running headlong and borrowing $14 billion unnecessarily, but nevertheless it is being borrowed. It indicates a real insensitivity to the small business community. In fact, this insensitivity was demonstrated in the last few weeks when we were looking at the marginal manufacturing tax in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

April 3, 1981
Borrowing Authority Act, 1981-82
This is an opportunity for the federal government to obtain revenues, but the confusion which exists in the business community over the marginal manufacturing tax is quite unbelievable. The fine tuning is not being done before the fact, it is being done after. There are a great many people who did not recognize that they were marginal manufacturers. They now find themselves in a situation where they must revise their plans for the future, they must revise their inventory development plans. Yet they still do not know the fine points within that legislation. They phone the Department of Revenue and the Department of Finance for clarification, and even then grey areas exist. These areas are being fine-tuned, now, when in fact this legislation will be effective as of January 1, 1981.
We would be much better off if we gave the business community a clear indication about this new method of obtaining revenue for the federal government and told the community that the measure will be in effect as of January 1, 1982. This would give them an opportunity to adjust to this tax which will be coming their way. This is the kind of sensitivity that many of us would like to see from the federal government, particularly as it relates to the small business community.
One can say, "Oh well, not all is lost. The government did provide some assistance to the small business community; they brought in the Small Business Development Bond." Unfortunately, when you look at the small print and the restrictions associated with that bill, you see that 95 per cent of all small businesses in Canada are prevented from taking advantage of the Small Business Development Bond. When you look very closely at the mechanics of that particular bond, you will find that the real beneficiaries are not the small entrepreneurs of Canada or the small businesses across the country but the chartered banks. The lending institutions are the ones which really benefit from the Small Business Development Bond, not the small entrepreneur.
When considering the $14 billion that we are being asked to authorize today, we recognize that none of this money will be used for new programs, new projects or new opportunities for Canadians. It will be used simply to service the existing debt. One must ask the question: What is this money being used for?
Contrary to the opinion of many of us in this House, and those of us who read the front pages of the newspapers, particularly here in central Canada, who get the impression that the main problem today is the Constitution, that that is the subject on everyone's mind, it is not the case. When you get out into the community and talk to the men and women in your constituency, you find that patriation, amending formulas, and so on, are not the topic of priority. In fact, the priority is how mortgage payments will be met, how living costs and food costs will be met. Inflation is seen to be in the 11 per cent plus range and wage increases in the last round of contracts have been 11 per cent, 8 per cent-which is less than the cost of living. The people know the effect that these figures will have on their lives and the lives of their children. They are concerned about this. They are also concerned about government expenditures. They look at this kind of bill, a bill to borrow $14 billion, and they ask what the money is being spent on. They ask what the new plans of this government are, and how it will get the economy back on track.
If there is one thing that all the best economists in this country agree upon, it is industrialization. They look at the countries in the western world and see that they are all industrializing, even the underdeveloped and developing countries.There is one country in the world which is de-industrializing, and that country is Canada. We are de-industrializing at a time when all the good economists of the world see other countries industrializing. What on earth is our plan? What is our economic blueprint for the next decade? The simple answer is that we have none. We do not have an industrial strategy. We do not have a manufacturing or transportation strategy. What we need is a revision of our spending to include a measure such as the one the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) brought forward a number of months ago in the House. We must clearly distinguish between those items termed government spending and those termed government investment.

FREE VOTE ON REINSTATEMENT Mr. Scott Fennell (Ontario) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of allowing a free vote in the House of Commons on the reinstatement of capital punishment for first degree murder.
He said: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It was a pleasant surprise for me, not only to speak twice in this House in one day but also to finally see my motion come before the House for debate.
I am called a guillotine man. I think you will find, as I go through my debate, that I am really not. The motion I put
Capital Punishment
forward is an extremely important concern, more so to my constituents than to myself. We are continually accused of being sheep, of being herded and of only voting the party line. What I am proposing in this motion is that capital punishment should be put on the floor of the House as a free vote, totally free, no party affiliation, no party controls. Usually we are frightened of the criticism of our leader and the repercussions therefrom. I believe that this should be a free vote and not a contrived or controlled vote. It is a situation which is of great concern to many of our citizens, both those who are opposed to capital punishment and those who are in favour of it.
Since I have been a member of this House, there have actually been two cold blooded murders in one part of my riding. The first one occurred shortly after I was elected in May, 1979.1 received a phone call concerning it. A very young policeman was murdered. His young wife was left with two very young children; one was yet a baby in her arms. This hit home with me, as I had met this man during the election. He had run up to me in the street and said, "Please, Mr. Fennell, what is your stand on capital punishment?" I listened to him, and he explained the fears of the members of the police department. I said, "That is important to me. I will definitely go to my constituency to find out how all my constituents feel." I did this, and the results were that 87 per cent were in favour of capital punishment. This young man was killed at short range while performing his duties as a policeman protecting the innocent citizens of this country. It was hard to go to his funeral, as I realized that only a few weeks before I had talked with this man on the street.
The second murder happened only last fall. It was rather tragic because a young lady, 21 years of age, was not only molested but was also murdered. Her body was thrown behind a sign board alongside a main street in one of the towns in my riding. Nobody knew what had happened to her until the next morning when children who were going to school found this body and reported it to the police. These were young children of public school age who were shocked by this.
This act was committed by an accused man about whom I have already written to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan). This man was out on bail. In checking with the Durham Regional Police Department, I found it had never been notified that he had been allowed out on bail. In checking with his parole office, I found it had never been notified that he was out on interim bail. It was while this man was out on bail that he committed this crime upon one of my constituents.
What will stop these crimes? What is the deterrent? I have heard all the "goodie" side, which suggests it is not a deterrent. Yet between the years 1961 and 1978, the rates of crime have doubled. We have tried this route, and found it not to have been effective. That is why I brought this motion forward.
I do not believe in capital punishment. I do not believe in the way it is carried out. However, we must deter these terrible criminals who are a threat to our society. One keeps hearing that it is not a deterrent, that it is, it is not. I am convinced by statistics.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
April 3, 1981
Capital Punishment
The hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) spoke to me this afternoon. He said, "I am glad you are up. I am sorry I will not be here because in my riding alone the crime has increased 23 per cent this year." It is increasing everywhere. Crime is on an upswing and the tragedy is that we have lost our morality.
Minor offenders realize that there is really no penalty for breaking a window and stealing out of a store, sticking a toy gun in a shopkeeper's stomach. We are not dealing with the most serious crimes of the land: cold-blooded murder and molesting. Those must be dealt with. We must do something. We are doing nothing. We are sitting on our buttocks and acting like a bunch of sheep. We will not stand on our own feet and do something.
It is important to bring a bill before this House quickly before it is too late. If you look at Section 12 of the resolution on the Constitution, it clearly states there that capital punishment would be removed forever from our law books. Believe me, we will never change that Constitution. Equal rights amendment people in the United States have tried for years but have not been able to change it. So we had better do something quickly because it is our last shot and our last chance.
I am sure that all of you received-some of you may not have read it-a letter from the attorney general for the province of Ontario. He has given a prime example of what we are doing to the people of this country. It concerned a case in the United States where certain information was not admissible. I am not a lawyer so I cannot give the technical explanation. This was a case where a young girl went to a basketball tournament with her family. She subsequently went to the washroom and did not return. The only clue as to what had happened was that a young man saw a man carry something in a garbage bag out of the door. The man was subsequently identified and caught. After the police picked him up, his rights were read to him, and he was told that he was believed to be at fault. He told them, "If you are that convinced, I'll take you to the body." So he took them to the body of this child whom he had molested and killed. Hon. members have all read about this and know that it had happened in the United States. The courts would not accept that as admissible evidence because he did not have a lawyer with him at the time, even though he had voluntarily admitted to the crime.
Those are the kinds of people we are allowing to walk the streets of this land. I hope we do not entrench that section in our ill-conceived Constitution. At the beginning I mentioned that I did a survey in my riding. Actually I had a response from 87 per cent of the population. I had a large return. I believe 2,200 people answered my query. Some of them expressed their view against capital punishment. Many of them expressed their view for it. They are concerned with putting some teeth back in the law. That was really the message which came through: "Please, will you get morality back in this country? We have lost it. We let those terrible people away with anything they want to do. They walk the
streets." That was their feeling and those are the people on whose behalf I am speaking. They are scared, they are frightened. Do not let our cities turn into cities like Detroit, Cleveland or the northeastern cities where thousands of murders occur each year. We are lucky in this country. We are fortunate that our people are much more passive. However, we could change. Crowded conditions in cities create a dangerous situation.
I would like to ask the hon. members of this House how they would have felt if we, as Canadians, had had to endure and witness what happened to the Americans in October of 1963 in Dallas or on Monday of this week in Washington. Do we want one of those murderers to go to prison for a short term or do we want to attempt to deter him from doing it again? Would we want him out walking the streets again? Possibly the next time it could be one of the leaders of our country. I do not think we want that. We must stop it, and we must stop it now. How would hon. members feel if it was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? I do not believe that this would appeal to anyone in this House. This epitomizes the danger of allowing these people to run free. I am sure all hon. members would stand on their feet and speak out if anything like that were to happen. In our hearts we would look at what we are doing. We would look beyond our prejudices and we would listen to our constituents. I believe if that kind of a situation happened here, and pray to God it never does, we would be reconsidering our stand. We all have consciences. Hon. members know that, I know that, and if something like that did happen here, it would really touch my heart and my conscience.
We cannot let these people go free. We cannot keep them in jail. It is an injustice to a person to incarcerate him for 25 or 50 years. What are we going to do? Many of these murderers are in jail. The man in Utah who recently went to the gas chamber is a perfect example. Before going to the gas chamber, he said, "Please, I do not want a reprieve. My life is over".
In my motion I am referring only to premeditated, coldblooded murder and high treason. We must do something about these crimes.
I have heard the argument that we should put the matter to a referendum. In my opinion this is a chicken-hearted way for this House of Commons to deal with it. It is passing the buck to the people who have elected us. I, for one, am not in favour of a referendum. I say we are the people who represent our constituents and we must stand up with our feet firmly on the ground and make our own statements. We should not be chicken-hearted and go back to the people asking them to do it for us. It is the same thing as using a referendum for the Constitution. I am against that. It is our responsibility. People want to enjoy their lives, people want to work. They do not have time to do all the reading and studying that we do. It is our responsibility to make decisions here in a democratic way.
Earlier on I mentioned the guillotine man. Let me say, in response to that age old accusation of being a hangman, that I would propose, in conjunction with this bill, that the reintro-
April 3, 1981

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
duction of capital punishment be subject to the use of a more humane method. I believe there are humane ways. I believe there are easy ways. I was a farmer. I had sick cattle that I could not cure. I had crazy bulls I could not cure. They were dangerous. There was a very simple procedure, but I hated to use it because I have a hard time hurting anything, even an ant, but I used it. There is a humane method, and everyone knows there is.
People who commit crimes are sick, incurable souls who go out and perpetrate the same act again and are a danger to our society.
I plead with the members of this House today to consider my motion if we have an opportunity to vote on it. It is very clearly stated as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of allowing a free vote in the House of Commons on the reinstatement of capital punishment for first degree murder.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell). I am somewhat surprised at the attack he made on his colleague, the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) who has a motion on the Order Paper which specifically provides:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of holding a national referendum on the issue of capital punishment and, following such referendum, should amend the appropriate sections of the Criminal Code to conform with the majority views of the people of Canada.
I would say to the hon. member for Ontario that he had better check with his colleague about this matter. When motion No. 4 comes up, I expect the hon. member will give the somewhat strident argument he gave today against the idea of a referendum. Frankly, I happen to agree with him. I do not think that is the way to resolve a problem of this nature. There has been a lot of talk about surveys. I often wonder about the days of Wilberforce. He wanted to abolish slavery. If he had taken a survey in his riding, or for that matter anywhere in England, at the time the odds probably would have been that slavery was okay, and it probably would have been approved by 90 per cent of the population. It was only through showing leadership that people of his stature were able to bring to the attention of the public they were serving that abolition of slavery was a step forward. Any referendum or survey taken at that time would certainly have been against what Wilberforce was endeavouring to do.
I agree with the hon. member, as this House has agreed on several occasions, that votes on such subjects should be free votes. In the time that I have been here since 1968, give or take the hiatus from 1979 to 1980, we have heard some splendid arguments. Some of the better debates in the House of Commons have come about as a result of free votes in the House. The last free vote I participated in was at the initiative of the then solicitor general. We had not only a good debate and heard forceful arguments on both sides, because there are cases to be made for both sides, but in the final analysis, this Parliament, this House of Commons to its credit saw fit to vote against and abolish capital punishment, we hoped and thought at that time, for all time.
Capital Punishment
It is of some interest to me that it was a Progressive Conservative who probably did more to convince me on this subject that abolition was right for the twentieth century. I had the pleasure on more than one occasion to listen to a very eminent Canadian, the Hon. Arthur Maloney, who spoke with feeling about this subject, about the need for this country to finally move into the twentieth century. Never again would the state be put in the position of taking the life of one of its citizens, whether we do it humanely by hanging, by electrocution, by the use of a guillotine, or by whatever other method.
The hon. member made the point that some of these people are sick and incurable. Surely they are not the ones we should be putting to death. Those, of all people, are the ones we should be helping. Let us find out why they are sick and why they are incurable. By doing that, perhaps we can prevent other murders from taking place in the future. The hon. member, if he is fair, will recognize that no jury or court in this land will convict an individual who is sick and incurable and tell him he has to face the death penalty. This is not the way the system works.
I support a free vote totally. But it seems to me that those of us who believe in abolition, who believe the last vote taken was the correct one, find that the onus, if there is to be a change, should be on those who want a change.
I have been waiting for a motion to be put, but not in the general terms we have here: let us bring back the death penalty. We find though that those who are for capital punishment cannot get their act together. Some of them would have capital punishment for the murders of police officers, prison guards and political leaders. Others have different choices. We hear that anyone who carries a gun in the commission of a crime should be subject to capital punishment. Many of us argued as strenuously as we could, sometimes knowingly putting our own political careers on the line, because we take what seems to be an unpopular position in our riding, taken because we feel and we know in our hearts that it is right. Leadership does not come about by taking a survey and finding out what all of the people want, and then running around ahead of them, saying "follow me". Leadership, and [DOT] that is what we should be giving, calls for more than a survey and an indication about the way a member will vote because the people or the crowd are telling him to vote.
If we are going to have another debate on this subject, it is not up to those of us who believe in abolition to bring it forward. It is up to those who believe in capital punishment to see if they can get their act together, bring in a motion and try to have it carry in the House of Commons. That is not our responsibility. We fought our fight and are prepared to fight it again if need be. I do not intend to take the initiative to move away from what the House has already decided in a free vote.
On this particular subject, a tremendous amount of research has been done by those on both sides of the issue. It is interesting to note that in the last debate in the House in which I took part, approximately half the members of the

April 3, 1981
Capital Punishment
House participated. After a while the arguments on both sides took on a certain similarity. It was time to put the matter to a vote, which we did. I will concede that the vote was very close, but the majority of the members of the House of Commons, to their credit, voted. I said at the time that I hoped capital punishment would be abolished for all time. I think the vote was 130 to 124.
I know this subject interests many members of the House. For that reason I will not pursue it any further other than to say I cannot agree with the hon. member that this is something we should be doing, moving us back toward the nineteenth century rather toward the twenty-first century. It is a retrograde step. It is saying to what is now an enlightened society: let us move back a little into the shadows. This is what Canada wants in the twentieth and twenty-first century. We want to say to our children that we were involved and participated in that debate.
The hon. member says now we should hang the sick and the incurable. If we do that, we will start with all kinds of nonsense in this country. We made the decision in the last vote. I hope that vote will have the effect of abolishing capital punishment for all time.
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in hearing the last speaker degrade the matter of a referendum. It is going to be very interesting to see how he votes on referenda-

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I know the hon. member does not want to mislead the House. I was indicating that the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) was the one denigrating it. I said I hoped he would speak in as strident a voice about the motion put forward by his colleague from Erie who wants a referendum. I do not think a referendum is the right way to handle it.

I accept the statement of the hon. member. I hope I will be given an extra minute. I am sure he would not want to deprive me of that.
There are two sides to this question. As Sir Roger de Coverley said in the primary readers, much can be said on both sides. I support capital punishment. In my view, a large percentage of the people of Canada support it. In fact, well over 70 per cent do.
There are two philosophies. One was put forward by the last speaker who said we should provide leadership. That is said in many countries when government wants to tell the people what is good for them. I do not believe in that type of philosophy. I believe in providing leadership, but I also believe in reflecting the thinking of the people.
I was elected by a large majority of my constituents to support capital punishment. In a democracy, there is a responsibility on members to reflect the thinking of those who sent them here. One does not suddenly become knowledgeable because one happens to be elected. The origin of democracy was that since all the people could not go to Parliament, a few were sent to represent the thinking of the majority.
We are getting too far away from that today. We are telling the people what is good for them once we have been elected. When a person is elected, he does not have any more wisdom than he had before. The primary purpose of being elected is to reflect the thinking of the people. That is democracy, and that is what I am going to talk about now.
If I did not believe in capital punishment, I would have made it a point to tell that to my constituents at my nominating convention and throughout the election campaign. However, I do believe in capital punishment. I made a point of telling the people that if I was elected, I did not want them to ask me to oppose capital punishment because that is something I cannot do. I was elected on the basis of my conviction.
I want to deal with some of the reasons why I believe in capital punishment. This is a House of debate. The idea of debate is to endeavour to carry the judgment of other people, not to tell them what is good for them. I respect the view of the last speaker. I do not agree with it, but I respect it.
When he was referring to the sick, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) was not asking that those who are insane be subjected to capital punishment. That is not what he intended. No court will convict someone who is sick.
When I talk about capital punishment, I want to define it right from the beginning. I am talking about the death penalty for the murderer of another human being who has deliberately planned and killed a person and has been found guilty in the courts beyond the shadow of a doubt. That is the type of person who should suffer the death penalty. Let me tell you why.
When I was a child, I was punished if I did something wrong. If I did something worse, I was punished more severely. We accept punishment in our homes. It is a necessary part of upbringing.
One time a minister of the gospel came to me to tell me that he did not believe in bringing death to another individual. I asked him if he would punish his child if he stole something. He said yes, absolutely. When I asked him whether he would punish his child more severely if he stole to a greater degree, he said yes. When I asked if the degree of punishment would continue based on the wrong that was done, he said yes. I asked why he would stop when a person commits the ultimate crime and the ultimate sin of taking the life of another human being. He stopped and reflected, but he did not give me an answer.
I believe that capital punishment is the ultimate punishment for the ultimate crime. When a person in his right mind deliberately plans and kills another human being and is found guilty in the courts beyond the shadow of a doubt, he too should be executed. I will not deal with the method of execution. That may vary. However, he should be executed.
Let me go into this a little further and discuss whether it is a deterrent. I believe it is a deterrent because we all love life. We do not want to die. Very seldom do you come across someone who wants to die. We all want to live because we love life. Why should we assume that someone who takes the life of
April 3, 1981

another does not want to live? Love of life is a fact of life, and that is why some do not want the death penalty. I believe capital punishment is a definite deterrent to murder. The fear of death is instinctive.
Many people today will say they are ready to die. A very fine Christian woman spoke to me a short time ago saying she was prepared and ready to die. I asked her whether she wanted to die, and she replied, "No, no, I do not want to die but I am ready whenever the good Lord calls me." She loved life even though she was old and suffering from disease. We all regard life as a precious possession. People love to live.
Whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent is really irrelevant. It is utterly impossible to determine how many people were not killed because of the fear of the death penalty. We know how many people have been murdered, but we do not know how many were not killed for this reason. The argument, either way, therefore, is inconclusive. My idea is that the fact that people fear death and love life makes capital punishment a realistic deterrent.
Let me deal with this point a little further. In our society today, many people are becoming concerned with the extent of unlawfulness, and unruliness. Some have come to the conclusion that the only possible deterrent to the brutality committed in this country and throughout the world is the reinstatement of capital punishment in those countries where it does not now exist.
A few weeks ago, the world was shocked by the senseless and brutal murder of John Lennon. I was not a particular fan of John Lennon's but I was horrified that he had been shot. He actually did not sing the kinds of songs or play the kind of music I like best, but I was sorry that this artist had been brutally killed. I immediately asked why this had been so, and came to the conclusion it was senseless. What do we say to a person who deliberately commits that kind of murder? I think the answer to that question is that the death penalty will be applied in respect of those who plan that type of thing.
The hon. member for Ontario mentioned the senseless shooting in Washington the other day. If the man is insane, that is one consideration, but, on the evidence so far, the indication is that he was completely sane, knew what he was doing, planned the event and carried it out deliberately. He had the gun and he was ready for the event.
I have a number of nephews who are police officers. When I go back to Alberta or visit British Columbia I am never sure whether they are still alive. Every day police officers take chances with their lives in order to preserve order for you and me. Hundreds of young men and young women in the RCMP and in our city and village police forces take their lives in their hands when they put on their uniforms. They become the targets of those who deliberately want to break the law.
I know of one police officer who spent several weeks tracking down a murderer. He was finally successful; the man was charged and brought to court. The judge said to him, "You" know, this was bad; this was not good. Do not do that again.
Capital Punishment
The court let him off on probation. Recently a policeman in Calgary was killed by someone who was let go free.
On one occasion I asked a convicted murderer whether the fact that he had taken a human life bothered him. His reply was: "No, and I would do it again." The man was guilty of a crime of passion, but he said he would do it again. I wondered, as I looked at that man, whether I would want him living next door to my house after he was released from his short term behind bars. Would I want him living in an area where there are innocent boys and girls? My answer is, of course, that I would not, and I do not think any members in this place would want him living near them.
These convicted people do not stay in prison for very long, and that creates a problem. Today we have between 100 and 200 murderers in our prisons. I sympathize with the difficulties facing our Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan). The penitentiary in Drumheller in my constituency is supposed to be a medium security prison, but for some time now officials have been putting individuals who belong in a very strongly guarded environment along with those who should be in a medium security prison. Exactly what happens when you put bad apples with good apples? I have never heard of bad apples turning good but I have often seen good apples turn bad.
A young man in the penitentiary I just mentioned said to me on one occasion when I visited him, "I hate it here. I am learning more about how to commit crime than I ever thought there was to know." It is for this reason I recommended to the Solicitor General that we should not put those who should be in tight security in medium security prisons.
What are we to do with these 100 or 200 murderers? They have killed once. They spend 12 years, 15 years or 20 years in prison if they go the full term. Some of them are fairly young and have quite a bit of life left. They know the death penalty has been abolished in Canada so there is no deterrent to them not to kill.
Let me return to the consideration of capital punishment as a deterrent. The individual who deliberately takes the life of another human being, is found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and meets the death penalty, will never murder anybody else. Fathers and mothers do not have to worry about that man harming their sons and daughters. People in Toronto, Calgary or any of our large city centres are concerned for the safety of their children. Senior citizens in most of our urban centres are afraid to go out in the streets at night.
The death penalty is symbolic. It is a warning to those who break the law that they will be punished; if they commit the ultimate crime they will face the ultimate punishment. Do not tell me that anyone in his right mind cannot understand that. Capital punishment is a deterrent. It would not be much of a deterrent in the case of a killing as a result of an argument in a bedroom or a bar room. These killings occur without any planning or deliberation, so perhaps there is not much of a deterrent there. Those things just come up. No one is saying there would be a deterrent in such cases. Such crimes of passion are beyond reason. However, in my view, capital punishment is a deterrent to those who would deliberately plan

April 3, 1981
Capital Punishment
the death of other persons. Canadian statistics indicate that if a robber, burglar or rapist knew with reasonable certainty that killing his victim would result in his own execution, he would think twice about it. 1 know that is not a very good example, but newspaper stories I have read with respect to the yellow dogs who killed the shoeshine boy in Toronto have told about what they said in court about discussing the matter before they killed that little boy. One of them gave evidence in court and said that they discussed the fact that there was no death penalty, and that was one of the reasons they killed that little boy. Today the taxpayers of this country are keeping them in prison. I suppose the taxpayers are keeping them pretty well because the bleeding hearts of this country make sure they have their televisions, radios, entertainment and their good times.
Colour television.

Colour television, yes, which many people cannot afford.
I believe in rehabilitating people, but let us make sure we have a chance to rehabilitate someone who has committed the ultimate crime before we attempt rehabilitation. In this country today many Canadians are digusted because we are concerned more about those who kill than we are about their victims. We sometimes forget about the little boy, the little girl, the police officer, the guard or the man or woman. I do not care who it is; if he or she is deliberately killed by someone who thinks it out, plans it and schedules it, in my view that person is ready for the death penalty, and he should face it.
To come back to the motion, what we want is a free vote because this is not a matter for parties to decide. It is a matter on which members should reflect the thinking of the people who sent them here. It is a moral matter. I do not know of any party which has taken a definite stand one way or the other. There are probably people in all the parties of this country who take one side or the other, but a free vote would reflect the thinking of the people, and we would be carrying out real democracy.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) ought to be congratulated for having brought forward this motion. Today is a good day because it is really the first day on which Parliament has started working normally again. It is very refreshing to be back to normal business after seven or eight days of having to listen to some 60 phony, empty and meaningless questions of privilege-

-most of which were rejected by Madam Speaker. I am happy to see something of substance and concern to Canadians at large being brought forward. It is in this sense that I offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Ontario. It is very reassuring that we are back again to
normal business. Let us hope that we will not be distracted in the days and weeks to come by the intentions expressed only a few days ago by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) when he said in this very House-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the hon. member, the item before us is a private member's bill dealing with capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on this bill; the hon. member can speak on that at another time.

I am coming to the point. I am trying to establish the importance and the constructive nature of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Ontario, in contrast to what his colleagues have done for the past seven days. It seems to me to be a very legitimate point that we are not today wasting parliamentary time as advocated on March 27 by the hon. member for-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I very, very seldom intervene in a debate such as this, but the hon. member has been called to order two or three times by Your Honour, and he ought at least to have the courtesy to recognize Your Honour's challenge and stick to the point.

Mr. Speaker, having made that point, I would like to say to the hon. member for Ontario that we in this House have done exactly what he has advocated. We did have a free vote. The hon. member is shaking his head, probably because he was not present. I remember that the galleries were packed that day. The atmosphere was tense. Everyone knew that it was a very historic moment. Mr. Speaker, you were also in this House. We knew it was quite an important moment. We voted. It was a free vote, so much so that there were hon. members opposite who voted for abolition and hon. members on the government side who voted against abolition. It was a truly free vote. In a sense, every party broke up because every member voted according to his or her conscience. It was quite an historic day. As the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) mentioned a few moments ago, it was a very close vote. The motion passed by only some six or seven votes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if I may ask the hon. member if he would keep the record straight. He said that every party broke up. Our party members voted each as he chose, but it just so happened that we were unanimous in our opposition to capital punishment.

I thank the hon. member for having produced that additional element of historic precision. I am very grateful for that. I suppose he is very proud of that, and quite rightly so.
The speakers on the side of the hon. member for Ontario seem to live under the impression and notion that capital punishment would once and for all eliminate, or at least reduce, murder. That is an erroneous notion. It is disproved by the fact that in countries where there is a capital punishment there is a high murder rate. In countries where there is no
April 3, 1981

capital punishment there tends to be a lower murder rate. In other words, the two are not related, as proved by the fact that even last Monday when we witnessed on television with horror what happened in Washington, we know that in most of the states south of the border there is capital punishment, yet that did not prevent that man from shooting and attempting to kill. It did not prevent another man in 1968 from shooting and killing Robert Kennedy. It did not prevent another one from shooting and killing President Kennedy. It did not prevent another person, in 1975, from attempting to murder President Ford. Yet in most of the states south of the border there is capital punishment. So I ask, what does it do? Is it a deterrent? Hon. members opposite have not discharged the onus of proving to us that it is. They have just said-as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) says he believes-that it is a deterrent. The hon. member for Bow River has not produced any evidence or any proof.
South of the border is the classic example. There is capital punishment in most of the states, and yet there is a high rate of attempted murder and murder. Is there a deterrent? If we knew there was, we would look at the matter in an attempt to solve the problem for society and to eliminate the constant occurrence of tragic events, as described so well by the hon. member for Ontario and the hon. member for Bow River. We do not want that to happen and we have to find the answers. But those who believe capital punishment is a deterrent have the responsibility to prove it with facts, not with sensation, feelings or belief, as desirable and moving that approach may be. It needs more proof because the history of mankind is filled with instances, some cases in the United States, where it turned out that an innocent person had been executed.
We hear the hon. member for Ontario telling us about humane methods, the way he applies it to his bull and his cow. Perhaps he fails to realize that there is a distinction between an animal and a human being, or perhaps, in his opinion, there is no distinction, in which case that is where we part ways. Those of us who participated in the free vote he advocates, believe in and prefer by far a humanistic approach until it can be demonstrated that there is a deterrent, which has not been proven, otherwise this House, when we had the vote last time, would have arrived by means of reasoning at the inevitable conclusion that there should be capital punishment. But those who wanted capital punishment failed to prove this is a deterrent and that is why they lost.
On the eve of the twenty-first century, in trying to solve this problem that has been with us since the very beginning, we have to come to the conclusion that prevention is the route to follow. Preventive measures such as gun control have their limitations because we all know that they are not that effective. Prevention should be attempted by way of social measures at the neighbourhood level, in the schools and in family life, so that harmonious and healthy family situations from birth enable youngsters to grow up in a healthy environment. These and other measures on the preventive side should be undertak-
Capital Punishment
en, rather than trying to cure a situation after the problem has occurred and a life has been lost.
What the member for Bow River is asking in essence is that the state cold-bloodedly execute one of its citizen, as the member for Sarnia put it so well. The hon. member says: you kill, I kill, and we all kill in the name of the collectivity because that is the best way we can come to grips with this dramatic, tragic and difficult situation that not only affects Canada but affects every society in the world.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that in those nations where capital punishment has been eliminated, the crime rate has not been affected. Abolition of capital punishment is an important recognition that capital punishment is not a deterrent, and I challenge the hon. members who have spoken before me to prove with facts that it is. I would be most interested in hearing this evidence, which has to be a result of thorough study and analysis of whether or not there is a relationship between capital punishment and murder rates. The onus of proving that is on the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Ontario, if they really believe that human beings should be treated like the bull and the cow because that is the way he does it on his farm when he has sick animals in the field.
That is not what he said.

That is the essence of the message, Mr. Speaker. The point really is whether capital punishment also brings in its wake a serious element of injustice, if one looks at what has happened in other jurisdictions over the years. At the time of debate in this House when we had a free vote, as advocated by the hon. member for Ontario-
Why the smile?

-there were no whips on, everybody was free to vote according to his or her conscience. Many Conservative members voted for abolition and, if they were free to vote, the same thing applied to Liberals who voted for the retention of capital punishment, because there were some on this side who voted that way. So a free vote has taken place.
However, the question that comes to mind is the element of injustice, which has been raised by other speakers. What we are going through here today, Mr. Speaker, is really an echo of a debate that took place in this chamber many years ago. In a way we are convering the same ground because, unfortunately, and this perhaps is a sad conclusion, in the years that have gone by since 1976 we have discovered nothing new about this phenomenon. At that time, the majority of members voted freely in this chamber, and I repeat the word "freely" because it does not seem to get through to the hon. member for Ontario. But the only difference between him and me was that he was not in this House whereas I was.
The measure as such brings in its wake an element of injustice because there have been a number of cases in history, as I mentioned earlier, as in the case of people who have been

Of course, the inevitable question that no one can answer is: how do you bring back to life someone who has been wrongly executed? How do you apply a law that will inevitably fall more heavily on those who are uneducated, on those who are probably mentally sick, on those-
